seoTitle: Create Horizontal Scrolling Images in Squarespace
metaDescription: Build a horizontal scrolling image gallery in Squarespace with a Slideshow layout, thumbnails, and autoplay, using the built-in section editor.
intro: A horizontal scrolling image gallery reads as far more polished than a static grid of photos, and Squarespace builds the whole thing from a single Images section — no plugin, no custom code. The part that isn't obvious the first time through is that the gallery starts life as a grid, and it's a gallery type setting buried in the section editor that actually turns it into a scrolling slideshow with thumbnails and autoplay. This guide walks the real editor screens for adding the section, switching its layout, and dialing in the thumbnails, autoplay, and pacing that make it feel finished.

steps.heading: Add an Images section to your page
steps.body: From the page editor, click Add a Section to open Squarespace's content picker, which groups options like Digital Products, Scheduling, Donations, Images, Videos, Menus, Forms, Charts, and Audio. Choose Images, and you're shown a set of pre-built layout starting points — some built around a large hero-style photo with brand copy overlaid, others pairing a smaller image with a text block — any of which works as your gallery's starting point since you'll change the layout type in the next step anyway.

image.caption: The Add a Section panel, with Images listed among the content types you can drop onto a page.

steps.heading: Switch the gallery type to a Slideshow
steps.body: Once your images are loaded into the section, open its settings panel and look at Gallery Type. By default it's set to Grid: Simple, but the same dropdown includes Grid: Strips, Grid: Masonry, and three slideshow variants — Slideshow: Simple, Slideshow: Full, and Slideshow: Reel. Any of the Slideshow options is what converts the static grid into a horizontally scrolling presentation; which one you pick depends on how large you want each image to appear as it scrolls past.

image.caption: The Gallery Type dropdown, showing Grid: Simple selected alongside the Slideshow: Simple, Full, and Reel options below it.

steps.heading: Set the height, width, and thumbnail strip
steps.body: With a slideshow type selected, the panel switches to slideshow-specific controls: Controls Location for where the previous/next arrows sit, Height presets from S to a custom size, and a Width slider that controls how much of the section each slide fills — 80 out of 100 leaves a bit of surrounding space so the image doesn't feel cropped tight to the edges. The Thumbnails toggle beneath these adds a strip of preview images below the main slide, which gives visitors a way to jump straight to a specific photo instead of clicking through one at a time.

image.caption: The slideshow's size controls — Height, Width at 80, and a Thumbnails toggle — beneath the main preview image.

steps.heading: Turn on autoplay and set the pace
steps.body: Scrolling further down the same panel, Autoplay is what makes the gallery advance on its own instead of waiting for a visitor to click through manually, and Slide Duration controls how many seconds each image stays on screen before the next one loads — 1.5 seconds is fast and punchy, while a higher value gives each photo more time to register. With Thumbnails and Autoplay both switched on, the gallery shows the current slide large, a strip of clickable thumbnails underneath, and advances automatically at whatever pace you've set.

image.caption: Thumbnails and Autoplay both enabled, with Slide Duration set to 1.5 seconds and the thumbnail strip visible under the main image.

steps.heading: Tune the duration for your content
steps.body: A slide duration under two seconds suits a fast-moving showcase of many small products, while anything with detail worth studying — a portfolio piece, a before-and-after photo — reads better closer to three or four seconds. There's no universal right answer here; scrub the duration slider and watch the preview scroll at that pace before deciding, since what feels right depends entirely on how much visitors need to actually look at each image.

steps.heading: Decide whether captions and dividers add or distract
steps.body: The same settings panel includes a Captions toggle and, further down, styling options like a section Divider with different shape presets. Captions are worth turning on if your images need context a viewer wouldn't get from the photo alone; leave them off for a purely visual showcase where text would just clutter the frame. The divider shape is a cosmetic flourish for separating this section from whatever comes next on the page, and it's easy to preview a few options since they update live as you click through them.

steps.heading: Preview and publish
steps.body: Before publishing, switch the editor's preview to the mobile icon at the top to confirm the slideshow scrolls and autoplays the same way on a phone screen, since gallery sections can behave differently at narrow widths. Once it looks right in both views, save the section and publish the page — the gallery goes live exactly as configured, no separate embed or plugin step required.

faq.question: Does Squarespace support autoplay for image galleries?
faq.answer: Yes — once you switch the Gallery Type to one of the Slideshow options, an Autoplay toggle and a Slide Duration control appear in the section settings.

faq.question: What's the difference between grid and slideshow layouts?
faq.answer: Grid layouts (Simple, Strips, Masonry) display images in a static arrangement, while the Slideshow layouts (Simple, Full, Reel) create a scrolling, sequential presentation with autoplay and thumbnail options.

faq.question: Can I show thumbnails alongside the main slideshow?
faq.answer: Yes — turning on the Thumbnails toggle adds a preview strip below the main image so visitors can jump to a specific photo.

faq.question: How do I control how fast the slideshow moves?
faq.answer: Adjust the Slide Duration setting in the gallery section settings — lower values move faster, higher values give each image more time on screen.

faq.question: Which slideshow type should I use?
faq.answer: Slideshow: Simple, Full, and Reel differ mainly in how large each image renders as it scrolls; try each against your actual photos since the right choice depends on their aspect ratio and how much detail they need to show.
